problem: Social robot navigation (SocNav) has no agreed-upon benchmarking protocol: papers use heterogeneous metrics, baselines, and rarely human surveys, which can lead to contradictory or poorly supported conclusions.
motivation: Without a de facto standard, researchers do not know which algorithms to compare against, which metrics to use, or how to decide when metrics disagree. The authors therefore systematically review recent benchmarking practice (Jan 2020 to Jul 2025) to quantify this heterogeneity.
key_idea: A PRISMA-style short methodological review of 85 SocNav algorithm papers from IEEE Xplore that audits which metrics, baselines, human surveys and claim-drawing practices are used in benchmarking.
insight: Benchmarking practice is highly fragmented: 52.2% of papers gave no rationale for their metrics, 35.8% gave none for their baselines, and 38 of 85 used no social metric at all. Claims of superiority mostly rest on few metrics or few baselines (22 of 26 used 2 or fewer), and 32.7% admit no method wins on all metrics, so conclusions are fragile. Human surveys are rare (18.9%) and seldom include third-party baselines (7.1%).
method: Search: IEEE Xplore query ("social robot navigation" OR "social navigation"), Jan 2020 to Jul 2025, returning 130 papers, all document types.
Screening: two-stage, each paper screened by two authors. Excluded 8 for topic relevance and 44 for having no navigation algorithm contribution, leaving 85 papers (65%).
Extraction: for each paper, recorded quantitative navigation metrics, baseline algorithms, use of human surveys, and how conclusions were drawn.

Normalisation rules: metrics that measure a phenomenon or its absence, or that differ only by a threshold, were merged; weighted-average metrics were split into components; ablations and parameter-only variants were treated as the same algorithm; comparisons to dataset pedestrians or a human-operated robot were ignored.

Outputs: a metric taxonomy table (social vs non-social, grouped by measured variable), a Sankey diagram linking metrics, papers and baselines, a table of survey questions, and a categorisation of claim types.
numbers_note: Literature review with no navigation benchmark results of its own; only survey statistics.
results: Of 85 papers, 53 (62.4%) compared against third-party algorithms, 77.6% used non-social metrics and 54.1% used social metrics (47.1% both). The most common social metrics were DH_min, SC, PC and C_risk. The most common baselines were ORCA, DWA, SFM, CADRL, SARL, CrowdNav and LSTM-RL, and CrowdNav was the only baseline created since 2020 that the reviewed papers used.
limitations: Only IEEE Xplore was searched, so coverage is not comprehensive and papers on other platforms are missed.
Metric and algorithm grouping rules involve subjective choices, and the review does not propose or validate a concrete standard benchmark.
builds_on: Francis et al. principles of social robot navigation benchmarking
